titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Thursday, 5 January 1922
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Miss Weaver: I find I shall have to draw another £50 of that sum for my own expenses as no money is likely to come in from subscribers before the end of the month so that I shall be glad if you will send on that amount on receipt of this – that is, if that is the arrangement you made. I forget whether you said I was to write to you or to your solicitors and if I attempted to look for your letter in my present condition of nerves and papers I should have to abandon work for the day. Yesterday Mr Liveright (of the New York firm Boni and Liveright) asked me to meet him. He wants to acquire from Mr Huebsch the American rights of my first novel and offered to give me an advance of $1000 on a 25% royalty for the American rights of Ulysses . I did not take it but advised him to wait and read the book in its complete form and see how it is received. You may keep that plan and the Secolo . In a few days if I am less fatigued I shall try to make one for the Oxen of the Sun which seems to give you a great deal of trouble. I sent you the proofs (made in advance uncorrected and with omissions) for Ithaca which however I should like to have back when you read them. The printing of Ulysses is finished. I have still work of revision to do but I have made a vow that I will not write a word more of it after 1 February. Enclosed is a cutting Mr Larbaud sent me. As usual it contains fantastic exaggerations. I send you also a cutting from a Dublin newspaper which speaks for itself and is an answer to the first of the seven heads of indictment which have been drawn up against Ulysses .

Many thanks for your Christmas and New Year wishes. I hope they and the Greek flag which I have hanging beside the fireplace will bring me luck and health and repose – from which you will deduce that I am extremely fond of myself. I renew my wishes to yourself. I hope to summon up sufficient courage in the spring to go to London – when the waters have subsided a little after the launch of a certain dreadnought.
With many thanks. Kindest regards and apologies for this tired letter.

postscript.p: P.S. I think it would be well to send marked copies of that Observer number to:

John Quinn, 31 Nassau Street, New York
Carlo Linati
Dr Geber, Gebersforlag, Stockholm.

div.note: Boni and Liveright, a New York-based publisher established in 1917 by Albert Boni and Horace Liveright, attempted to publish Ulysses in 1922, before giving up due to legal difficulties.
A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.

The so-called “schema” of Ulysses, an outline of the themes associated with each episode, mentioned also in JJ’s letters to Larbaud of 6 November 1921 (LIII 53), 15 November 1921 (LIII 53), and 26 November 1921 (LIII 54).
Probably Il Secolo (18 November 1921): 3, sent to Weaver on 10 December 1921 (SL 287). The newspaper had published the article “Un Ulisse irlandese” by Triestine journalist and editor Silvio Benco.
Probably the article titled “Ulysses: James Joyce and his chef d’oeuvre”, The Observer (11 December 1921): 9.

On 7 December 1921, Valery Larbaud gave a séance on Ulysses in Adrienne Monnier’s Paris bookshop, La Maison des Amis des Livres. Here Larbaud delivered a lecture in anticipation of, and in close resemblance to, his forthcoming review in the Nouvelle Revue Française .
In February 1921, the editors of The Little Review, Margaret Anderson and Jane Heap, were tried for obscenity for publishing the “Nausicaa” episode in their journal’s April 1920 issue.
“Ulysses: James Joyce and his chef d’oeuvre”, The Observer (11 December 1921): 9.
In 1921 Hugo Gebers Förlag in Stockholm had published a Swedish translation of A Portrait.
